t.3.65.1: Having thus offered water to him, the two Rāghavas then set out, and searching the forest for Sītā, they went toward the western quarter.
t.3.65.2: Having gone toward that southern quarter, the two Aikṣvākas, bearing arrows, bows and swords, set out upon an untrodden path.
t.3.65.4: Having swiftly passed on and taken the southern direction, the two mighty ones went across that very terrible great forest.
t.3.65.3: It was entwined with many shrubs, trees and creepers, covered on every side, impassable, dense and dreadful to behold.
t.3.65.5: Then, having gone three krośas beyond Janasthāna, the two Rāghavas of great vigor entered the dense Krauñca forest.
t.3.65.7: Longing to see Vaidehī, the two of them searched that forest, halting here and there, worn down by the abduction of Sītā.
t.3.65.6: It looked like a dense mass of many kinds of clouds and seemed to rejoice on every side, filled with lovely flowers of many colours and with herds of deer and flocks of birds.
t.3.65.8: But Lakṣmaṇa, of great splendour, steadfast, virtuous and pure, with joined palms spoke these words to his brother of blazing splendour.
t.3.65.9: My arm throbs violently, and my mind seems agitated; and for the most part I perceive inauspicious omens.
t.3.65.11: This bird called Vañculaka, exceedingly fierce, is crying out loudly, as if proclaiming our victory in battle.
t.3.65.10: Therefore, O noble one, make yourself ready and heed my beneficial words, for the omens are announcing at once a sudden alarm to me alone.
t.3.65.12: As the two of them were thus searching that whole forest with vigour, a great sound arose, as if it were shattering that forest.
t.3.65.13: The dense thicket seemed to be violently wrapped about by the wind, and the sound of that forest arose as though filling the very sky.
t.3.65.14: Seeking the source of that sound, Rāma, together with his younger brother, saw in the thicket a rākṣasa of enormous body and broad chest.
t.3.65.15: Then the two of them came upon Kabandha standing there before them, huge, without head or neck, his mouth set in his belly.
t.3.65.16: Covered with dense, sharp hairs, he towered like a great mountain; fierce and resembling a dark cloud, he roared with a sound like the rumbling of thunderclouds.
t.3.65.17: He had a single terrible eye set in his chest, tawny, broad and long, fringed with great lashes and swift of sight.
t.3.65.18: Him, furnished with huge fangs, large-mouthed and ceaselessly licking his lips, devouring exceedingly fearsome bears, lions, deer and elephants.
t.3.65.19: Him, brandishing his two terrible arms, each stretched a yojana long, and seizing with his hands bears, flocks of birds and beasts of many kinds.
t.3.65.20: They saw him dragging in and tearing apart many leaders of the deer herds, standing there blocking the path of the two brothers as they approached.
t.3.65.21: Then the two, having gone on a distance of only a krośa, saw Kabandha, huge, cruel and terrifying, enveloped by his arms.
t.3.65.22: That mighty-armed one, stretching out his two vast arms to their utmost, seized the two Rāghavas together, squeezing them with force.
t.3.65.24: The mighty-armed Kabandha, foremost of the Dānavas, said to the two of them: "Who are you two, with shoulders like bulls, bearing great swords and bows?"
t.3.65.23: The two brothers, sword-bearing and armed with sturdy bows, of fierce splendour, mighty-armed and of great strength, were being dragged along and had fallen into helplessness.
t.3.65.25: You two have reached this dreadful region and have come before me as my food. Tell me what your business is here, and for what purpose you two have come.
t.3.65.26: You two have come to this region where I stand tormented by hunger; armed with arrows, bows and swords, like a pair of sharp-horned bulls, you have arrived right into my mouth, and life will be hard for you to win back again.
t.3.65.27: Having heard those words of the evil-minded Kabandha, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa with a face that was drying up.
t.3.65.29: Great indeed is the might of Time over all beings, O Lakṣmaṇa; see, O tiger among men, how you and I are both bewildered by misfortunes. Nothing is too heavy a burden for fate among all beings, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.65.28: O you of true valour, passing from hardship to a still greater hardship, a dreadful calamity has now come upon me that will end my life, for I have not found my beloved.
t.3.65.30: Even the brave, the mighty, and those skilled in weapons, when seized by Time on the field of battle, sink down like bridges made of sand.
t.3.65.31: Speaking thus, the glorious and majestic Dāśarathi, firm and true in his valour, looked at Saumitri of lofty prowess and then, by himself, made his own resolve steadfast.
